title: Year three close: the story and the circle
hookLine: a long line from Jericho to Lagos, and a year that keeps turning

cards: Twelve stones, piled up near Jericho. Each was carried on a man's shoulder from the dry riverbed where the priests stood, one man for each tribe. Joshua tells them the stones are for the children.
That was near the start of this year: Israel crossing the Jordan.
From there the story ran a long line, through judges and kings, exile and return, apostles and martyrs, monks and reformers, all the way to churches in Lagos.
Then the line bent into a circle: the church's year of feasts, from Advent candles to a king crowned with thorns. Today, both close.

teach.b: The first was a line: Israel's story from Joshua to the return from exile; the early church, its martyrs and its creeds; the middle centuries, east and west, cathedrals and crusades, mystics and plague; the reformations, Protestant and Catholic, with saints and failures on both sides; then the church spreading across the world, to Lagos and far beyond.
A line has a direction. It says: this happened, then this, and it matters what came first. The second shape was a circle.
These last weeks walked the church year: Advent and Christmas, Lent and Easter, Pentecost, saints' days, All Souls, Christ the King. A circle comes round again.
In Western churches, the first Advent candle will soon be lit again. Ecclesiastes knew both shapes: "One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever."
The generations are the line. The earth and its seasons are the circle. Back to the stones by the Jordan.

teach.h: WHAT MEAN YE BY THESE STONES?
teach.b: Joshua says they are a sign, so that "when your children ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean ye by these stones?" someone will tell them the story.
That's how the line keeps going: a child asks, and someone answers. And that's why the circle matters: every year the feasts come round, and the story is told again.
The psalm puts it in one breath: "One generation shall praise thy works to another." The line hasn't ended. The circle keeps turning.
And somewhere on both, there's a spot marked today.

how: Western churches that follow the church year mark its turning at Advent (the Orthodox year begins on 1 September), and some end the old year with Christ the King and begin the new one with the first Advent candle, telling the same story again.

practice: Let the year pass by, from the river stones to the churches in Lagos and the candles and feasts, and ask where you are in it today: inside it, beside it, at the door, still deciding; all of those are places.
Find one honest sentence that says where you stand, and write it down. If you pray, you can offer that sentence to God; if you don't, just keep it.

wordCard.voice: Ecclesiastes. The Bible's book of the turning seasons, which knew both shapes this year walked: a line, and a circle.

carryVoice: Your line: the circle turns. Tomorrow, year four begins: many rooms, and how people talk about God. Year three, done.
